backups.name: Berdeen Peak Scramble
gear: sturdy mountaineering boots or scrambling approach shoes
ice axe (seasonal, if approach gullies hold snow)

long committing approach
backups.overview: Berdeen Peak rises above remote, turquoise Berdeen Lake in the Bacon Creek drainage of North Cascades National Park, about 1.25 miles east of 7,080-ft Hagan Mountain, within the NPS-designated 'Berdeen' cross-country zone. There is no trail: the peak is reached by a long, brushy off-trail approach from the end of Bacon Creek Road (Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF) near Marblemount, followed by a Class 3 (occasional low Class 4) scramble up the east ridge and NW slopes. It is seldom climbed as a standalone objective — most parties take it as the opening summit of longer Northern Pickets-area ridge traverses, such as the multi-day 'Mystery Ridge' enchainment (Berdeen-Hagan-Mystery-Pioneer-Crowder-Swiss-Whatcom-Easy-Mineral).
backups.beta: The only documented ascent (Abegg's party, Aug 2012) climbed directly over the peak's east side and NW slopes rather than contouring around a subsidiary spur, finding mostly Class 3 terrain that is 'steep and mossy' with one or two unavoidable Class 4 moves; careful selection of moss and rock holds was needed on loose ground. Reported Day 1 stats for the full push from the road (including the Porkbelly Ridge approach and a descent to camp beyond the summit) were +6,550 ft / -1,820 ft over 6.3 miles — most of that gain occurs on the way to Berdeen's summit, with the loss coming afterward on the descent toward camp, so treat the raw numbers as slightly inclusive of travel past the summit rather than a pure car-to-summit figure.
backups.turnaround: Given the long, pathless brush approach up Porkbelly Ridge, no cell coverage, and no nearby trail or rescue infrastructure, set a firm turnaround time based on remaining daylight and weather — down-climbing the loose, mossy Class 3-4 terrain in the dark or in rain adds significant risk with no easy retreat option.
backups.comms: No cell coverage is documented for this area; it lies deep in North Cascades National Park backcountry, far from any highway or repeater. Treat the entire objective as no-signal and plan/communicate accordingly (e.g., a filed itinerary or satellite communicator).
backups.descent: Reverse the ascent route back to the Berdeen Lake basin, then retrace the Porkbelly Ridge bushwhack to Bacon Creek Road.

backups.detailed_rack: No technical rack is used on this route. The only detailed trip report of an actual Berdeen Peak ascent (a Mystery Ridge enchainment approaching via Porkbelly Ridge and the east side/NW slopes) describes mostly Class 3 terrain with one or two Class 4 moves on steep, mossy, loose rock, and does not mention a rope, harness, or any protection being placed or carried for the summit scramble itself.

backups.pro_needs: None needed — this is an unroped Class 3-4 scramble. The limiting factor is loose, mossy rock and careful hold selection, not a lack of protectable terrain, so gear is a non-issue; a helmet is the main protective item worth carrying given the reported rockfall/handhold-failure hazard.
backups.approach: From the end of Bacon Creek Road (~850 ft, Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF), an intermittent boot path continues briefly along the old roadbed and the east-bank benches of Bacon Creek before angling up onto Porkbelly Ridge, the broad forested spur that climbs northeast toward Berdeen Peak. There is no maintained, numbered trail here — this is an unofficial climbers'-path/bushwhack route — and tread comes and goes through slide alder, vine maple, and devil's club in the lower timber, easing somewhat in open forest and heather bands higher up. Porkbelly Ridge is one of the brushiest approach ridges in this part of the range, so treat the brush-fighting and route-finding through it as the day's real crux, not the scrambling above. Bacon Creek, crossed or paralleled within the first mile or so above the road-end, is the last easy, reliable water; above that, plan on carrying water or relying on occasional seeps/lingering snow patches until you're near Berdeen Lake. The ridge gains steadily and steeply — roughly 6,550 ft of cumulative gain and 6.3 miles are logged for the full push from the road-end, over Berdeen Peak, and down to a camp above Berdeen Lake, which lines up with this route's recorded ~5,600 ft/23 km round-trip scale. Higher up, the ridge passes from brush into subalpine parkland and then rock/heather benches below Berdeen Peak's east side. One line contours around the summit on a spur ridge to avoid the top entirely, but most parties instead climb directly over the 6,400–6,420 ft summit via the east ridge/east side: easy-to-moderate terrain, mostly low Class 3 with occasional short Class 4 moves on steep, mossy rock, where holds need to be chosen carefully since moss-covered rock is slick, especially wet. Loose blocks and exposed dirt/heather steps along the ridge crest are the main scramble-specific hazards; a helmet is worth carrying. Near the summit, Berdeen Lake's turquoise basin opens up to the north/northwest. North-facing terrain along the approach ridge can hold lingering snow well into midsummer.
backups.descent_text: This is a scramble descent with no rappelling — walk/downclimb off, either back down the ascent line or via the peak's northwest slopes, which is how most parties link the summit to a camp above Berdeen Lake. From the top, descend the NW slopes on moderate Class 2–3 dirt, heather, and broken rock, losing roughly 500 ft to the basin above the lake, then rejoin the Porkbelly Ridge line to reverse the bushwhack back down through parkland and timber to Bacon Creek and the road-end trailhead. Stay on or near the ridge crest as long as practical on the way down — dropping off-ridge into the brushier side-drainages or the creek gully below adds substantial extra bushwhacking and is a common way to lose time. Loose, mossy rock immediately below the summit and steep brush lower on the ridge are the main hazards; because both the approach and the return are slow, brushy going, budget a genuinely full, strenuous day (or plan on the overnight camp above Berdeen Lake that most trip reports use) rather than treating this as a quick out-and-back. Parties continuing into a longer traverse (Hagan Mountain, Mystery Ridge, the Pickets) push on past Berdeen Lake instead of returning to the trailhead same-day.
backups.bail: From the east ridge or NW slopes, downclimb/retreat the way you came to the Berdeen Lake basin; from there the only realistic exit is back down Porkbelly Ridge to the Bacon Creek Road end — there is no shorter bailout given the off-trail, roadless surroundings.

itinerary.cal: Best done July-September once the Porkbelly Ridge brush and upper ridge are snow-free; the drivable end of Bacon Creek Road can vary year to year with washouts, sometimes adding extra road-walking to the approach.

days.note: From the end of Bacon Creek Road (~850 ft) the route leaves the last road tread almost immediately and grinds straight up Porkbelly Ridge — trip reports call it one of the brushiest ridges in the range, with no consistent boot path despite published mentions of one. Push through brush, timber, and steep duff to a camp near treeline below Berdeen Peak, saving the summit scramble for fresh legs the next morning.

bivy.name: Berdeen Lake benches
bivy.notes: The camp for Berdeen Peak and the substance of the Bacon Creek side of this zone. The documented approach starts at the Bacon Creek road end at valley-bottom elevation, scrambles up Porkbelly Ridge, crosses the east side of the peak around 6,400 ft and drops to camp above the lake — a very big first day with four thousand feet of gain, much of it trackless. The lake sits in a deep cirque a little over a mile east of Hagan Mountain and drains east over an enormous waterfall into a tributary of Bacon Creek, which is the geography that settles the argument about which road it belongs to: it faces Bacon Creek, not Baker Lake. It can be reached from the Blum Lakes over the divide to the northwest, but that is a traverse variation for a party already committed to a long trip, not an approach. From camp Berdeen Peak's east ridge is the way up, and the ground south and west continues onto the Bacon massif. Season is roughly mid-July into September, held back at the front by snow on the ridge and at the back by short days on a route with no trail.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet streams, fed off the glaciers above and reliable all season. Treat it. This is the first dependable water since the valley bottom, over four thousand feet below.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, required for any overnight and written for a cross-country zone rather than a designated camp — a different thing to ask for, and it must be collected in person at the wilderness information center, which is a long way round on the far side of the range from the Anderson Creek trailheads. No campfires anywhere in the zone. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and never in the meadow, keep a hundred feet back from the water, and carry out human waste. A bear canister is the sensible answer where the heather gives you nothing to hang from; they can usually be borrowed at the permit office.
bivy.capacity: A handful of tent-sized spots on benches above the lake shore; the basin is large but the flat, durable ground is limited, and this is a cross-country zone with a small party cap rather than an established campground

bivy.name: Bacon Creek road end and Porkbelly Ridge
bivy.notes: There is no established camping on this approach and the honest answer is to start early and reach the lake basin in one push. The road leaves the highway a few miles east of Marblemount and runs up the valley to a road end around 850 ft, from which Porkbelly Ridge is climbed trackless — steep timber, deadfall and brush with better travel once the ridge crest establishes itself, and no benches, clearings or water worth the name in four thousand feet. The road is the first problem: it carries very large potholes over long stretches, a bridge on the main road beyond one of the side creeks has been out, and the spurs off it are variously blocked by missing bridges, washouts and downed timber, so how far a vehicle gets is a live question that changes year to year and adds miles at the bottom when it goes against you. A party that runs out of daylight on the ridge flattens a spot among the trees and moves at first light; that is the realistic use of this camp, not a plan. The same road end is the start for the Diobsud Creek side of Bacon Peak, which is climbed on a longer line past Salvation Peak with a glacier saddle camp around 6,250 ft — a spring and early summer objective needing snow travel gear, and a different proposition entirely from the summer scramble off the Anderson Creek road.
bivy.water: The creek near the road end, treated. Above it there is nothing dependable until the lake basin high on the ridge, so fill everything before you start climbing.
bivy.permit: The road end and the lower part of the ridge are Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, where a night in a pullout is generally tolerated and no permit is issued. The ground higher up crosses into North Cascades National Park, so if you sleep anywhere above the lower ridge you need a park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone. The boundary is not marked on the ground on this ridge, so ask at the permit office where it falls before planning a bivy rather than deciding on the hill. No campfires above the road, and total burn bans are common on this side through a dry August.
bivy.capacity: Rough parking at the road end and whatever flat ground you can find in the timber; one party, found rather than chosen. There is no camp here, and that is worth saying plainly.

backups.overview: New York Gully splits the NW Face of Snoqualmie Mountain, the most-climbed of five parallel ice/mixed lines on that wall (alongside Pineapple Express, Blue Moon, New York Gully Direct, and LA Express). First climbed by Ruch and Cordery-Cotter in 1985 as a IV 5.8 A2 WI4 aid line, it's a roughly 1,300-ft alpine route following a prominent gully system to a distinctive 'box gully' feature, finishing with a steep corner pitch that was originally aided and first freed in 2004 at M5+/6-.
backups.beta: A popular Seattle-area winter mixed testpiece: a short approach off I-90 leads to a moderate lower gully, then progressively steeper mixed ground (up to M5-) through slabby, sometimes loose rock, finishing at a splitter 5.8 corner crack that was historically aided (A1-2) and has since been free-climbed. Conditions vary widely year to year — some seasons build fat ice through the gully, dry years leave it mostly rock/mixed with minimal screw placements. It sits on the edge of the Phantom Slide avalanche path, so timing relative to snowpack stability is as important as the climbing itself.
backups.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time before starting based on remaining daylight, current avalanche danger on the Phantom Slide approach/exit, and how the party is moving on the mixed pitches — this is a committing gully route with limited fast bail options above the crux, so err toward retreating early if conditions, ice quality, or teammate pace are below expectations rather than pushing into the crux pitch late in the day.
backups.descent: From the top, most parties rappel from a tree anchor at a col between two gendarmes into the Enigma Gully (Slot couloir), then climb snow back up to the main summit ridge near 6,200 ft and walk the last bit to the summit. From there, descend the standard Southwest Slopes scramble route back to the Source Lake/Alpental trail, or, snow permitting, ski or boot back down the Phantom Slide to the resort. Round trip is commonly 8-11 hours car-to-car.

backups.detailed_rack: A single 60m rope plus a thin tag line (or a single 70m rope for simul-climbing sections) is standard. Rack to 2-3 inches including offset nuts and cams in the 0.2-0.5 in range for the P4/P5 dihedral and crack systems, a few knifeblade pitons for thin seams, and 3-4 ice screws (10-13cm) — screw count and size needs vary hugely with conditions, from essentially unnecessary in dry years to fully useful in a fat-ice season. No bolts on route; some fixed pitons exist at select stances. Bring extra slings for tree/horn anchors on the lower gully and for the walk-off.

backups.pro_needs: Protection is a mix of thin-crack gear (offsets, small cams, knifeblades) for the rock sections and screws for whatever ice is present that season; the crux corner crack takes good small-to-medium cams and was historically bridged with two moves of fixed-gear aid (A1-2) before being freed.
backups.best_season: Best after a solid early/mid-winter freeze builds ice in the box gully and the upper corner; a sustained cold snap in Dec-Jan usually gives the fattest ice, while warm or dry winters can leave the route thin, forcing dry-tooling on rock (per 2025 trip reports). The northwest aspect stays cold and holds what ice forms later into the season than sunnier Cascade lines.
backups.approach: Park in the Alpental groomer lot, about 200 ft past the main day-lot at the end of WA-906/Alpental Rd (reached via I-90 Exit 52). From the lot, walk up the open, south-facing hillside toward the Alpental waterfalls. At the base of the falls, cut left into the trees for roughly 100 ft and climb up through two steep, often snowed-up rock/cliff bands — this section is frequently booted or skinned by prior parties, and picking up an existing track through the thick timber makes a real difference in speed and route-finding; without one, expect slow going. After about 300 ft of gain, angle right onto the Phantom Slide itself, a broad avalanche path that is the defining feature (and hazard) of this approach: it slides regularly, including on skiers and climbers on the upper apron, so check the NWAC forecast beforehand and time your crossing/ascent to stable conditions rather than lingering on it. Climb the slide path to about 4,900 ft, then trend left and up through lower-angle, more open terrain to a notch on the NW shoulder/West Ridge near 5,200 ft. From the notch, downclimb roughly 200 vertical feet into the Thunder Creek cirque basin and traverse beneath the NW Face to the base of the gully system — note this face hosts five closely spaced ice/mixed lines (Pineapple Express, Blue Moon, New York Gully Direct, New York Gully, and LA Express), so confirm you're racking up below the correct one. No reliable water source along this approach in winter/spring conditions; plan to melt snow. Figure roughly 1.5–3 hours car-to-base depending on snowpack, track conditions, and party experience with the terrain.
backups.descent_text: From the top of the technical climbing (the crux mixed pitches, including the route's namesake 'box gully' section), downclimb easy snow angling to climber's right, then traverse up to a col between two gendarmes on the upper ridge. From that col, make one rappel from an established tree anchor — a single 60m rope reaches the bottom comfortably (many parties carry a 70m since it's also useful for simul-climbing/leading the route's 4 long pitches), dropping into the Enigma Gully, also known locally as the Slot couloir. This tree-anchor rappel is also the standard bail point if weather, conditions, or time force a retreat before topping out. From the base of the rappel, climb back up moderate snow in the Enigma/Slot gully to regain the main summit ridge near 6,200 ft, then walk the short remaining distance to Snoqualmie Mountain's true summit. From the summit, descend the standard Southwest Slopes scramble route: steep, loose scree and exposed rock past Cave Ridge, dropping toward the Source Lake basin and rejoining the Snow Lake/Source Lake trail back to the Alpental parking lot (this standard descent line is roughly 3,100 ft of its own elevation loss over about 1.9 miles one-way, and is considered a genuinely hard, sustained scramble in its own right, not just a walk-down). In good, stable snow conditions some parties instead ski or boot straight back down the Phantom Slide to the resort rather than taking the scree-and-scramble Southwest Slopes line. Total rappels on route: 1. Round trip is commonly 8–11 hours car-to-car.
backups.bail: The col rappel into the Enigma Gully can be used to bail before the crux pitch; lower on the route, parties can generally downclimb/retreat the approach gully back toward the Phantom Slide in stable conditions.

pitch_detail.notes: Follows a snow gully/bench just below a rocky bulge with a steep drop below; often simul-climbed with pitch 2.
Traverses up and left across the face on thin snow over rock to a short snow/rock gully ending at a dead snag below the box gully.
The 'box gully' crux: climbs straight up through a 3-sided box cave feature protected by pins and cams; the crux corner above was originally aided and first freed in 2004 at M5+/6-.
A short ice step (takes a 10cm screw) leads to a traverse across a snow ledge to a fixed multi-piece anchor.

days.note: Climbed car-to-car in a single long day. Parties hike from the Alpental lot up past the waterfalls through two steep snowed-up cliff bands to the base of the gully (the 'Phantom Slide' approach), then climb 4-6 pitches of ice/mixed/snow (crux typically a mixed step in the M4-M5 range) to a col below the summit ridge. From there most parties rappel from a tree anchor into Enigma Gully (the Slot Couloir), climb the snow back up, and descend the standard southwest slopes to the car.

approach_variants.name: Alpental groomer lot, the Phantom Slide, and the NW shoulder notch into Thunder Creek cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the groomer lot about 200 ft past the main Alpental day lot. Walk up the open south-facing hillside toward the Alpental waterfalls. At the foot of the falls, cut left into the trees for roughly 100 ft and climb through two steep, usually snowed-up cliff bands. After about 300 ft of gain, move back right onto the Phantom Slide.

The Phantom Slide is a broad avalanche path that slides regularly, including on people on the upper apron. Check the NWAC forecast and time the crossing rather than lingering on it.

Climb the slide to about 4,900 ft, then trend up and left through more open ground to a notch on the northwest shoulder near 5,200 ft. Reckon roughly one and a half to three hours car to base, and much of that depends on whether a skin track already exists — most of the approach is through thick trees.

No water on this approach in winter; melt snow.
approach_variants.season: Roughly December to March. A sustained cold snap usually gives the fattest ice; warm or dry winters leave it thin and force dry-tooling
hazards: The Phantom Slide is an active avalanche path and the approach crosses and climbs it
Five closely spaced lines on one face — racking up below the wrong one is the routine error
Loose, chossy rock on pitch two and through the box gully
Thin or absent ice most winters; be ready to dry-tool rather than swing
A cold, shaded northwest aspect with winter temperatures at the belays even on clear days
Alpental ski patrol conducts explosive avalanche control nearby
The descent finishes down the Southwest Slopes scramble, itself 3,100 ft of steep loose ground, or back down the Phantom Slide
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the notch, downclimb about 200 vertical feet and traverse to the first obvious gully. That is the published test and it is the one that works in cloud, because it is counted rather than seen: you are not identifying a gully by its shape from a distance, you are walking beneath the face from a fixed point and taking the first one you meet.

Why that matters here more than anywhere else on this page: this face carries five closely spaced ice and mixed lines — Pineapple Express, Blue Moon, New York Gully Direct, New York Gully and LA Express — and they are near enough together that racking up under the wrong one is the normal failure. Count from the notch, do not pick by appearance.

The pitch-one confirmation, and it is a good one: ascend roughly 200 ft up the gully and then take an obvious ramp out to the left, belaying from a quasi-cave. Gully, then a left-trending ramp, then a cave belay. If your first rope length does not offer a left ramp at about 200 ft, you are in a neighbouring line.

The second confirmation is higher and unambiguous: the route runs up obvious weaknesses to a small headwall split by a 5.8 crack, historically aided and now freed. That crack is the route's signature. A line with no headwall crack is not New York Gully.

And a honest warning about the approach itself: most of it is through thick timber and the published advice is to go with somebody who knows it or follow an existing skin track. Without a track, expect it to be slow and to be the part of the day where you lose time.

backups.overview: Set above the head of Cascade Pass near Spider-Formidable country, Magic Mountain (7,610 ft) is a rewarding scramble usually combined with a backcountry camp in the basin below. The South Ridge / Southeast Slopes standard route leaves Cascade Pass on a climber's path that traverses heather and talus below Mixup Peak's east slopes to the small Cache Glacier and Cache Col (6,900 ft), then descends a rising traverse SSE to Kool-Aid Lake (6,120 ft), a popular camp at the start of the Ptarmigan Traverse. From camp the route climbs about 1,000 ft directly up heather and scree to the saddle between Magic Mountain and Hurry-up Peak, follows an easy heather ridge to a false summit (roughly 300 ft SE of, and slightly lower than, the true summit), then drops about 80 ft to gain Class 3-4 broken, corkscrewing ledges on the NE face leading to the true summit. First climbed in 1938 by Calder Bressler, Ray Clough, Bill Cox, and Tom Myers.
backups.beta: From Kool-Aid Lake, descend about 600 ft on the Ptarmigan Traverse path, then traverse and climb to a 7,100 ft col east of the lake. From that col, ascend the South Ridge on heather and rock (Class 3) toward a false summit roughly 50 ft below and southeast of the true summit. Drop off the false summit and cross broken, exposed Class 3-4 ledges/gully on the east side of the summit tower to reach the true summit; fresh snow can force a detour into the summit moat.
backups.turnaround: Turn around before committing to the exposed ledges/gully past the false summit if the party lacks a comfortable time and weather margin to reverse the full traverse over Cache Col and back to Cascade Pass before dark or before incoming weather; fresh snow on the summit ledges or on the Cache Glacier traverse is a reasonable turnaround trigger.
backups.face: South Ridge, gained from the col between Magic Mountain and Hurry-up Peak; summit block climbed on its NE face
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: Cell coverage in this part of North Cascades National Park is unreliable to nonexistent per NPS guidance; do not rely on a phone for emergency communication, and consider carrying a PLB or satellite messenger.
backups.descent: Reverse the ascent: NE-face ledges to the saddle, then back over Kool-Aid Lake and Cache Col to Cascade Pass.

glacier travel and moderate-angle snow (Cache Glacier)
exposed class 3-4 scrambling near the false summit

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Road's-end trailhead on Cascade River Road (23.1 mi gravel from Marblemount); NPS wilderness permit required for camps beyond Cascade Pass.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is at the very end of Cascade River Road (FR-15), about 23.1 miles of gravel road from Marblemount, at roughly 3,600 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park here. Overnight parties also need a North Cascades backcountry camping permit for Kool-Aid Lake, picked up in person in Marblemount before you drive out.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Maintained trail tops out here; leave it for the unmaintained climber's path bearing SSE toward Cache Glacier.
waypoints.directions: The Cascade Pass Trail is well-graded and heavily switchbacked the whole way, 3.7 miles and about 1,700 ft to the notch between Mixup Peak and Cascade Peak. It melts out by early to mid summer and is the busiest stretch of the trip, since it is a popular day hike in its own right. Nothing here needs route-finding; the work starts at the pass.

waypoints.name: Cache Glacier toe / Mixup Peak traverse
waypoints.note: Rising traverse on snow or heather across Mixup Peak's east flank to the base of Cache Glacier; isolated crevasses and firm morning snow can require an axe.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the pass and pick up a climber's path bearing south-southeast, making a rising traverse across open heather and snow benches on Mixup Peak's east flank. The path is intermittent and vanishes entirely under early-season snow, so this is where navigation starts to matter. It brings you to the toe of the Cache Glacier around 6,000 ft, where firm morning snow makes an ice axe worth its weight.

waypoints.name: Cache Col
waypoints.note: Glaciated gap atop Cache Glacier between Magic Mountain and Mixup Peak; descend SSE from here toward Kool-Aid Lake.
waypoints.directions: Ascend the glacier on moderate snow, steepening to about 35 degrees near the top, to reach the col. This glacier is small and generally free of significant crevasse hazard, but it is still a snow slope with runout below, so crampons are worth carrying depending on season and how firm it is.

waypoints.name: Kool-Aid Lake
waypoints.note: Small tarn with established bivy sites used as base camp for the peak; outlet is snowbound and unreliable for water into early summer.
waypoints.directions: From the col the route drops rather than climbs: a climber's path makes a descending traverse to the southeast down to the lake. Do not continue north over the col. This is the last reliable water of the trip, and the outlet can still be snowbound into early summer, so fill here before going up.

waypoints.name: Magic Mountain–Hurry-up Peak col
waypoints.note: Climb roughly 1,000 ft from Kool-Aid Lake to this saddle, then gain Magic Mountain's south ridge toward the false summit.
waypoints.directions: From the lake the ground turns up again onto heather and scree leading east to the saddle between Magic Mountain and Hurry-Up Peak, where the South Ridge proper begins. There is no water at all above the lake, so leave camp carrying what you need. The slope is uniform and featureless in cloud, which is the only real navigational catch on this leg.

waypoints.name: Corkscrew ledges below false summit
waypoints.note: Past the false summit, drop about 80 ft down a loose gully to exposed Class 3-4 ledges that corkscrew the east side of the peak; a hand line or short belay is often used here.
waypoints.directions: Follow the South Ridge up on heather and rock at class 3 to a false summit, roughly 50 ft below and southeast of the true one. Do not try to stay on the crest from there. Drop about 50-80 ft down a loose, dirty gully on the far side to reach the ledge system, which is the technical crux of the whole outing.

waypoints.name: Magic Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit, marking the northern terminus of the Ptarmigan Traverse on the North Cascades NP / Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary.
waypoints.directions: The ledges are broken, exposed class 3-4 and corkscrew around the east side of the summit tower to the top. A hand line or a short belay is commonly used, and many parties rappel this section on the way down off a sling around a horn or chockstone, since there is no fixed hardware on this summit. Fresh snow can force a detour through the moat, and the loose rock means this section bites harder on the descent than on the way up.

backups.detailed_rack: A light rack of small to mid cams and a few nuts suffices for the summit moves.
pro_tips: Many parties combine Magic Mountain with the start of the Ptarmigan Traverse or nearby Spider-Formidable objectives, basing out of Kool-Aid Lake

The final miles of Cascade River Road are rough gravel and frequently washout-damaged; a high-clearance vehicle is recommended, and it's worth checking the NPS road-conditions page the day before you drive
watch_out: The climber's path from Cascade Pass toward Cache Col is unmaintained and easy to lose in poor visibility — many parties end up traversing too high or low on Mixup Peak's east slopes
The false summit is roughly 300 ft SE of, and lower than, the true high point — don't stop there
backups.pro_needs: Very light; protection is mostly for the final scramble.
backups.approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (3,660 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road (FR-15), follow the Cascade Pass Trail — a well-graded, heavily switchbacked National Park trail — 3.7 miles and about 1,700 ft of gain to Cascade Pass (5,360-5,400 ft), the low notch between Mixup Peak and Cascade Peak. This section is on-trail, well-marked, and passable by early-to-mid summer once the switchbacks melt out; it's also the most crowded stretch since it's a popular day hike in its own right. At the pass, leave the maintained trail and pick up a climber's path bearing south-southeast, making a rising traverse across open heather and snow benches on the east flank of Mixup Peak. This climber's trail is intermittent and route-finding becomes more important in early season when it's snow-covered. Continue the traverse to the base of the Cache Glacier (~6,000 ft), then ascend moderate snow slopes (up to about 35 degrees) to Cache Col (6,900-6,960 ft); the glacier here is small and generally reported free of significant crevasse hazard, but an ice axe and sometimes crampons are worth carrying for the snow slope depending on season and firmness. From Cache Col, descend roughly 600 ft on a climber's path with a descending traverse to the southeast, dropping to Kool-Aid Lake (about 6,120 ft), the standard camp/bivy area for Magic Mountain and the broader Ptarmigan Traverse. From Kool-Aid Lake, the final approach climbs about 1,000 ft directly up heather and scree slopes to the col (~7,100 ft) separating Magic Mountain from neighboring Hurry Up Peak, which is where the South Ridge proper begins. There is reliable water at Kool-Aid Lake and seasonal snowmelt along the traverse, but none on the upper ridge itself. A Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park at the trailhead and a backcountry camping permit is required from North Cascades National Park for overnight stays at Kool-Aid Lake; most parties treat this as a 2-day trip with a camp at the lake rather than a car-to-car push given the ~19-20 mile round trip and off-trail navigation.
backups.descent_text: Descent reverses the ascent line down the South Ridge. From the true summit (7,610 ft), climb back down the Class 3-4 broken ledges that corkscrew the east side of the summit tower, then climb back up the roughly 80 ft dirty gully to the false summit (about 300 ft southeast of the true summit) before continuing down the easy heather/scree of the South Ridge to the Magic Mountain-Hurry Up col. This corkscrew section is the technical crux of the whole outing — loose, broken rock with real exposure — and is where the route's single rappel comes in: many parties downclimb it as Class 3-4 with a spotting belay, but a short single-rope rappel (roughly 50-80 ft, well within a 30m or 60m single strand, or a doubled 30m rope) off a natural anchor — a sling around a horn or chockstone, since there are no bolts or fixed hardware reported on this remote, lightly-traveled summit — is commonly used by parties wanting to avoid down-climbing the loose ledges, especially in wet or snowy conditions. From the col, retrace the approach: down to Kool-Aid Lake, back up and over Cache Col, down the Cache Glacier snow slopes and the Mixup Peak traverse to Cascade Pass, then out the maintained Cascade Pass Trail to the trailhead. Watch for loose rock on the corkscrew ledges and the upper gully, and for soft/rotten snow on the Cache Glacier descent later in the day — this is a route best started early to avoid downclimbing softened snow on the return.
backups.bail: There is no faster alternate descent off Magic Mountain itself — the only way down is to reverse the South Ridge/Cache Col/Cascade Pass approach, so turn around early if weather is closing in or the Cache Glacier/Cache Col crossing looks unsafe rather than pushing for the summit.

pitch_detail.notes: Rising traverse on climber's trail/heather/snow across Mixup Peak's east flank to the Cache Glacier, then moderate snow to Cache Col (~6,900-6,960 ft).
Descending traverse SSE to Kool-Aid Lake (6,120 ft), the standard camp.
Ascend roughly 1,000 ft to the saddle between Magic Mountain and Hurry-Up Peak, then traverse/descend slightly to a 7,100 ft col east of Kool-Aid Lake.
Climb heather and rock on the South Ridge to a false summit roughly 50 ft below and southeast of the true summit.
Drop roughly 50-80 ft and cross exposed, broken ledges/gully on the east side of the summit block to reach the true summit; fresh snow can force a detour through the moat.

itinerary.cal: Cache Col and the upper approach typically hold snow into July; Kool-Aid Lake/Pelton Basin camping in North Cascades NP requires a wilderness permit (walk-up or advance quota in peak summer season).

days.note: From the Cascade Pass trailhead, switchback up the maintained trail to Cascade Pass, then leave trail and climb cross-country north to Cache Col. Descend snow/heather on the far side to Kool-Aid Lake (~6,120 ft), the standard camp for Magic Mountain and the Ptarmigan Traverse's southern end.

A few very fit, fast parties push it car-to-car in one very long (14-18 hr) day, but off-trail travel, route-finding on the ridge, and the wilderness permit make an overnight the standard approach.

access.fees: No National Park entrance fee. Wilderness permit: $10/person + $6 reservation fee if reserved via recreation.gov; free if self-issued at the trailhead.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: Backcountry wilderness permit required year-round for any overnight stay beyond the trailhead ($10/person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee if booked ahead on recreation.gov; free self-issue permits available at the trailhead kiosk when the Marblemount office is closed). approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass, Cache Col and Kool-Aid Lake
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cascade Pass trailhead at about 3,600 ft at the end of Cascade River Road, follow the maintained Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles and roughly 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at about 5,400 ft. This stretch is well graded, well marked and by far the busiest — it is a popular day hike in its own right.

At the pass, leave the maintained trail and pick up the climbers' path to climber's right, bearing south-southeast. It makes a rising traverse over snow or heather across the east flanks of Mixup Peak, crossing a spur ridge, to the base of the Cache Glacier at about 6,000 ft. The path is intermittent and in early season it is under snow, when route-finding matters more and the traverse has a bad runout.

Ascend moderate snow — up to about 35 degrees — to Cache Col at roughly 6,900-6,960 ft. The glacier here is small and generally reported free of significant crevasse hazard, but carry an axe and often crampons depending on firmness. Late season Cache Col itself can moat out and become awkward to cross.

From Cache Col make a descending traverse south-southeast, losing about 600 ft, to Kool-Aid Lake at about 6,120 ft — the standard camp for Magic Mountain and for the Ptarmigan Traverse, with reliable water. Most parties treat this as a two-day trip rather than a car-to-car push.

A Northwest Forest Pass covers the parking; overnight camping at Kool-Aid Lake needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, picked up in person at Marblemount for the Cascade River Road areas.

Cache Col moats out and becomes awkward late season
Loose rock on the summit tower ledges
The false summit — parties stop there or commit to the wrong side of it

approach_variants.baseFinding:
The South Ridge starts at the col between Magic Mountain and Hurry-Up Peak, at about 7,100 ft. From Kool-Aid Lake it is roughly 1,000 ft of straightforward heather and scree straight up to that col — there is no gully to pick and no notch to confuse, which makes this the most forgiving base on this list to arrive at.

The route-finding problem is not the base but the top, and it is worth knowing before you set off. The first third of the ridge is an easy heather scramble, with possible snow, leading to a false summit about 300 ft southeast of the true summit. That false summit is the landmark that tells you you are on route, and it is also where parties stop, believing they have topped out.

From the false summit the way on is counter-intuitive: find a dirty gully on the right and downclimb about 80 ft, then follow class 3-4 broken ledges that corkscrew around the east and northeast side of the summit tower. A hand line or a belay is worth having, and the descent goes back down the climbing route.

In poor visibility the two things to hold onto are that the col is the low point on the skyline between Magic and Hurry-Up, and that if you are standing on a high point with more rock still above you across a gap, you are on the false summit and need to lose height on the right before regaining it.

backups.overview: A little-visited summit on the Cascade Crest near Stevens Pass, WA. Spinnaker Peak rises above the headwaters of the Tye River between Lichtenberg Mountain and Tye Peak, about a mile from the Pacific Crest Trail. It's rarely climbed, largely because the surrounding terrain is a thick, brushy bushwhack once snow melts out; most parties instead treat it as an off-trail winter or spring snow climb, often paired with neighboring Martin Peak.
backups.beta: Two options exist to reach Spinnaker Peak's summit: the easier line climbs directly to the col between Point 5261 and Spinnaker Peak (steepest section of the trip, but low-exposure on the right line, and an ice axe isn't required if only Spinnaker is the objective); the harder option climbs Point 5261 first and follows the narrow, steeply-dropping ridge to Spinnaker's summit, which does require an ice axe and should be avoided in higher avalanche danger. backups.pro_needs: None. The route is non-technical; an ice axe is not required for Spinnaker alone, though many parties carry one for general snow travel or the connecting slopes to Martin Peak.
backups.best_season: Best climbed roughly December through April on a consolidated snowpack, when the brush and loose talus that otherwise cover this route are buried; spring (Mar-May) often gives the most reliable travel with corn-snow conditions. A summer ascent is explicitly not recommended by trip reports — thick vegetation and off-trail bushwhacking make the same line a slog once the snow is gone. backups.approach: Park at the Yodelin lot on US 2 (the former Yodelin ski area's lot, now used for overflow parking, roughly 1.7 miles from the Stevens Pass Ski Area pedestrian overpass, around milepost 60). Cross the highway and follow the old ski-area road south into the valley, staying near Nason Creek where crossings/snow bridges are most reliable, then continue into the open basin below the Spinnaker-Tye Peak ridge before turning up to the gap below Point 5261.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line back through the gap and down into the basin to the Nason Creek valley and the Yodelin lot. With a stable, consolidated snowpack the open basin can offer a quick glissade or snowshoe/ski descent, but avoid dropping onto the Pacific Crest Trail tread itself for winter travel — it crosses several avalanche paths near here.

approach_variants.notes: Park in the overflow lot off US-2 a couple of miles east of the ski area, cross the highway on foot and pick up the old ski-area access road into the valley, keeping near the creek where crossings and snow bridges are most reliable. Continue into the open basin below the Spinnaker-Tye ridge before turning up toward the gap. Almost every ascent is made on winter or spring snowpack; once the snow is gone this is a thick, unpleasant bushwhack that parties generally avoid, so the season is short and conditions-driven rather than weather-driven.

approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the climb is the col between Point 5261 and Spinnaker Peak. Coming up out of the basin, Point 5261 is the nearer rocky sub-summit and Spinnaker the higher point beyond it; the col is the low saddle between the two, and the ground rising out of it is the steepest of the whole trip although on a well-chosen line it carries little exposure and needs no axe if Spinnaker is your only objective. Take the col directly. The alternative — climbing Point 5261 first and following the connecting ridge across — is a materially different proposition: that crest is narrow, drops steeply into a series of small notches, ices over when windblown, wants an ice axe, and should be left alone with any avalanche danger about. So the check is simple: if you find yourself on a knife-edged crest with cornices and notches, you have taken the harder variant rather than the standard one, and the col is below and to your side. On the way down, keep off the trail tread itself for winter travel, since it crosses several avalanche paths near here.

bivy.name: The basin between Tye Peak and Spinnaker Peak
bivy.notes: A genuine winter camp rather than a summer one, and the natural base for Spinnaker Peak and its neighbour Martin Peak at the head of the Tye. The approach is from US 2 about two miles east of Stevens Pass, on the old road serving the Yodelin area, then up into the drainage on snowshoes or skis; the round trip to Spinnaker is around eight miles with a top out near 5,600 feet. From the basin the usual line traverses the northeast ridge past a subsidiary point around 5,300 feet, occasionally dropping onto the south side to avoid rock before regaining the crest. Parties combining Spinnaker with Tye Peak use this basin as the link between the two, which is the main argument for camping in it rather than doing either as a day trip. Everything here depends on snow cover — in summer the same ground is a slow thrash through slide alder and the peaks are seldom visited. Avalanche assessment is not optional; these are open, wind-loaded, lee slopes below a ridge crest, and the terrain traps in the drainage are real.
bivy.water: Melted snow in winter. In late summer the basin holds little or nothing reliable — carry what you need.
bivy.permit: National forest, no permit, no quota. Access from the highway east of the pass is across a mix of ownership near the old Yodelin development, so park on public ground and read the signs rather than assuming.

backups.overview: Mount Logan is a remote North Cascades summit. The Banded Glacier route is the standard line, ascending the glacier on the north side to a Class 3-4 scramble to the summit.
backups.beta: Approach via Easy Pass (6,500 ft) from Highway 20 mile 151, descend into Fisher Basin, then off-trail climb to Banded Glacier basin. approach_variants.notes:
Two ways in, and which one you use depends on whether SR-20 is open. The always-open option is the Thunder Creek trail from Colonial Creek Campground near 1,200 ft for about nine miles to the Fisher Creek trail junction, then the Fisher Creek trail about three miles — past a good log bridge with a handrail — to a lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier. Roughly thirteen miles one way. The shorter option is Easy Pass from SR-20 near milepost 151, over the pass at 6,500 ft and down into Fisher Basin, about ten miles, but the trailhead is gated by the highway's seasonal closure.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge — sometimes called Christmas Tree Col — which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the Banded Glacier on the far side and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.
hazards: A major crevasse crossed on a narrow snow bridge on the Banded Glacier
Talus lying on top of bullet-hard glacier ice, described as a pile of marbles — treacherous in a whiteout descent
Cliff bands above the lake camp
Loose chossy rock on the summit ridge and rockfall in the approach gullies
Heavy mosquitoes in the lake basin through June and July
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The critical transition is a negative test: gain the northeast ridge on solid rock at about 8,800 ft rather than attempting the summit block directly from the glacier. That is the base of the climbing and it is the single thing this route can get wrong. If you are trying to climb off the ice straight at the summit, you have skipped the transition — cross the glacier until you can step onto solid rock on the ridge, and only then start up.

Getting there is a sequence of two cols and they are different things. First, from the lake camp near 5,160 ft, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge — sometimes called Christmas Tree Col — and drop over it onto the Banded Glacier. Second, ascend the Banded to the Banded-Douglas Col, which is literally the saddle between the two named glaciers. A col you crossed to reach ice, and a col you reached by climbing ice, are not the same feature.

So the question that settles your position in fog is which glacier is under you: this route travels between two named glaciers, so if you can identify which one you are standing on, you know which stage you are at. The Banded is the one you drop onto from the ridge above camp; the Douglas is on the far side of the col above.

And all three Logan routes end on the same 300 ft of class 3-4 summit block, so the summit confirms nothing. What distinguishes them is entirely below: this one comes from Fisher Creek and a lake camp; the Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder; the Fremont Glacier route comes from Park Creek Pass on the other side of the mountain.

Watch the scree below the glacier on the way up with the descent in mind — it is unstable enough that parties note it climbs far better than it downclimbs.

backups.overview: Mount Prophet is a heavily forested, remote summit west of Ross Lake inside North Cascades National Park — Washington's 18th-most-prominent peak. The standard route is a long, brushy multi-day approach up Big Beaver Trail followed by a Class 2-3 scramble along the south/southeast ridge crest, with a short Class 3 step near the summit.
backups.beta: From a camp near Thirtynine Mile Creek/Thirtynine Mile Lake, parties push through brush alongside the creek to a relatively brush-free rib and climb to the south ridge crest around 6,600 ft. From there the route follows the ridgeline north over Pt. 6690, Pt. 7361, and the false summit at Pt. 7547 before finishing west to the true summit (7,640+ ft on USGS maps; 7,673 ft per modern LIDAR). Crestline travel is Class 1-2; the false summit and true summit involve steeper Class 3 rock with moderate exposure. Best done mid-to-late summer once the upper southwest cirque's talus/scree has melted out.
backups.turnaround: Set a firm early-to-mid-afternoon summit turnaround — there is no quick bailout once committed to the ridge crest, and July-August afternoon thunderstorms are common on this exposed terrain.

backups.descent: Reverse the south ridge and the brushy rib back down to Thirtynine Mile Creek, then follow Big Beaver Trail back to Ross Lake.

backups.approach: From Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20, MP 134) hike the Ross Lake shoreline trail ~7 mi to the Big Beaver Trail junction (or take the Ross Lake Resort water taxi to Big Beaver Landing to shorten this), then continue ~5 mi up Big Beaver Trail to Thirtynine Mile Creek/Camp. Leave the trail there and climb a brushy forested rib to gain the south ridge at a ~6,600 ft saddle. Round trip from the Big Beaver Landing water-taxi drop is roughly 18 miles with 7,000+ ft of elevation gain, typically done over 2-3 days; walking the lakeshore both ways instead adds about 14 miles. From the saddle, follow the ridge crest (Class 1-2) past points 7,361 ft and 7,547 ft to a short Class 3 step below the true summit; Luna Camp, about 5 miles farther up Big Beaver Trail, is the start of the separate Southwest Rib route, not this one.

backups.bail: Retreat along the ascent ridge is straightforward in good weather; in whiteout or fresh snow the Class 3 summit blocks and the brushy, cairn-less descent off the ridge into Thirtynine Mile Creek are the main routefinding traps. Track your ascent line (GPS) since there is no trail or marked route above Thirtynine Mile Creek.
backups.itinerary: Typically a 2-3 day trip: hike or water-taxi in to the Thirtynine Mile Creek area, high camp near 6,700 ft on the south ridge crest, summit day via the ridge, then exit back down Big Beaver Trail.

approach_variants.name: Big Beaver valley to Thirtynine Mile Creek, then the ridge
approach_variants.notes: From the Ross Dam Trailhead the trail drops to the lake and follows the shoreline to the Big Beaver Trail junction; a water taxi to the Big Beaver landing removes that shoreline stretch and is what most parties use. The Big Beaver Trail then runs up the valley through old growth to Thirtynine Mile Creek and its camp, which has tent sites on the west bank and a stock camp on the east, and is the last reliable running water and the last legal campsite before you leave the trail. Leave the tread between the creek crossing and the camp marker post and climb north through a brushy gully and the rib beside it — this low section is a genuinely horrible bushwhack and it is where the bulk of the day's gain happens. Travel eases considerably once you break out on the ridge crest above, where open forest and then open walking carry you over the intermediate points to the saddle where the rib meets the south ridge proper. An informal saddle campsite there splits the climb into two days, but it has no running water, so carry up from the creek.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, once the cornices on the south ridge have melted out and the talus in the upper cirque is clear.
hazards: route-finding through forest and along the ridge crest, with no marked line anywhere above the trail
cornices on the south ridge in early and mid season
afternoon thunderstorms on an open crest
a brushy, steep departure from the valley trail that is easy to lose in either direction
no water above Thirtynine Mile Creek
approach_variants.baseFinding: The highest point on the north-south crest is not the summit. Gain the south ridge at the saddle around 6,600 ft, where the brushy rib you climbed meets open crest. From there the travel is walking rather than climbing: follow the crest north over the first rounded point at about 6,690 ft, on to the rocky point at about 7,361 ft, and then to the point at about 7,547 ft. That last one is the false summit and it is the trap — it is the top of the north-south ridgeline and it looks final. The true summit is not on that line at all: from 7,547 turn west for a short distance, and the last few feet go at a short, steep scramble step with real but manageable exposure on both sides. So the test is directional. If you have topped out on the highest thing on the crest and there is still something higher a short way to the west, you are standing on the false summit and have not finished. If you are trying to climb something steep and sustained rather than walking a broad crest with two rocky steps, you have come up the wrong side of the ridge. The same short steps have to be downclimbed in reverse on the way out.

backups.fa: Dan Aylward & Forrest Murphy, July 3-4, 2004 (East Face, new route)

Crampons and ice axe for glacier crossing

backups.overview: East Face route on Poltergeist Pinnacle, the southernmost subsummit between Mount Challenger and Crooked Thumb in the Picket Range, approached via a glacier crossing to a dike-streaked granite shield. First climbed by Dan Aylward and Forrest Murphy, 2004.
backups.beta: P1's crux follows a dihedral into wild face climbing across parallel dikes to the shield's edge, unprotectable for roughly 40 feet before cracks appear halfway up (5.9, rated R for the runout). P2-P3 ease onto cleaner, better-protected corner systems with a small roof at mid-height; the upper ~800ft relents to low-fifth-class buttress-crest terrain, typically simul-climbed to the summit.
backups.turnaround: Because the route finishes by joining Mount Challenger's summit ridge and descending the crevassed Challenger Glacier, set a firm turnaround time that leaves enough daylight to complete the multi-hour glacier crossing back to Perfect Pass camp before dark, and budget for the multi-hour glacier approach from camp to the base of the route in both directions.
backups.rappels: No rappels needed on the route itself — descend by continuing over the ridge to Mount Challenger's main summit, then down the standard Challenger Glacier route (which has ~1 rappel on its final step)
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: No cell service anywhere on the approach or on the peak — North Cascades National Park backcountry is effectively a cellular dead zone. Carry a satellite messenger (e.g., Garmin inReach) or satellite phone for emergency communication.
backups.descent: Traverse the ridge crest north to Mount Challenger's true summit, then descend the standard Challenger Glacier route back to Perfect Pass.
obj_haz: loose rock on upper ridge/gully sections

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: From the end of the Hannegan Pass Road the route continues via Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack valley, Easy Ridge and Perfect Pass (~6300 ft) before a multi-mile crossing of the Challenger Glacier to reach the pinnacle.
waypoints.directions: Drive the Mount Baker Highway (SR 542) east from Glacier about 12.5 miles, turn left onto the Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32) and follow it about 5 miles to the trailhead at its end, where a Northwest Forest Pass is required to park. That is the end of the driving. Come prepared for a genuine multi-day trip rather than a long day, since this is one of the most remote and weather-exposed corners of the North Cascades with essentially no bailout options once you are committed.

backups.detailed_rack: A standard alpine trad rack: a single set of cams from small to about 3 inches (rock is generally sound and takes gear well on the upper pitches), a set of stoppers, and a handful of slings/draws. The first pitch is notably underprotected — the first-ascent party placed only a single small cam in the first 20 feet — so extra small/marginal gear and a willingness to run it out should be expected. Glacier-travel gear (crevasse-rescue kit, harness, prusiks, crampons, axe) is required for the Challenger Glacier approach and descent.
what_to_bring: Satellite communicator (no cell service in the backcountry)
Sun protection for extended glacier travel
Food storage/bear canister per NPS wilderness permit requirements
pro_tips: The first-ascent party had planned a different objective deeper in Luna Cirque but pivoted to Poltergeist Pinnacle when an icefall blocked their path — treat the glacier approach as committing and be ready to adapt your objective to conditions.

Secure your wilderness permit the day before if possible: the Glacier-area ranger station's earliest in-person pickup has historically been 8:00 a.m., which precludes a true alpine start on climbing day if you pick up the permit that morning.
The lower pitches climb dark granite streaked with prominent white dikes — the dikes offer some of the best holds and are a useful route-finding reference from below.
watch_out: Pitch 1 is rated 5.9+ R — protection is sparse for roughly the first 20 feet, and the first-ascent leader described the section as effectively soloed; a fall here risks a serious groundfall.
The 'Imperfect Impasse' below Whatcom Peak on the approach involves loose, exposed downclimbing (sometimes low 5th class); many parties rope up here.
Fog/whiteout is common on the glacier approach near Perfect Pass and can make navigation to camp difficult even close to the pass.
Crevasse hazard on the Challenger Glacier and around Challenger Arm, particularly in low-snow or late-season conditions.
backups.pro_needs: Standard alpine rack; placements on the crux first pitch are sparse and small, so the pitch should be treated as effectively R-rated regardless of rack size.
backups.best_season: Peak season in the Picket Range is a short summer window, roughly July through September, once high-elevation snow has consolidated enough for the Challenger Glacier crossing but before fall storms return; the first week of August is statistically the driest stretch of the year in the range. Early-season attempts should expect more snow on the glacier approach and possibly on the route and connecting ridge.
backups.approach: Drive the Mount Baker Highway (SR 542) east from Glacier about 12.5 miles and turn left onto the Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32), following it about 5 miles to the trailhead at its end; a Northwest Forest Pass is required to park. Hike the Hannegan Pass Trail about 4 miles to Hannegan Pass, drop into the Chilliwack River valley and cross the river, then climb onto Easy Ridge and follow its long, partly brushy climbers' path east. Cross the Imperfect Impasse, a moat-and-cliff notch that often needs a short low fifth-class downclimb, and climb snowfields to camp at Perfect Pass, roughly 16 miles and a full day from the car. From Perfect Pass, rope up, traverse around the Challenger Arm and cross about three miles of the crevassed Challenger Glacier to the base of the pinnacle. This is a genuine multi-day glacier expedition into one of the most remote, weather-exposed corners of the North Cascades, with essentially no bailout options once committed.
backups.descent_text: From the top of the technical climbing, simul-climb or belay short sections along the ridge crest (mostly low 5th class, up to 5.7) northward to Mount Challenger's main summit. From the true summit, descend the standard north-side Challenger Glacier route — the same line used for the peak's normal ascent — back down to Perfect Pass camp. Roped glacier travel is required; watch for crevasses, particularly late season as snow bridges deteriorate.
backups.bail: The lower three pitches offer limited retreat — gear anchors can be built at the P1/P2 and P2/P3 belays to rappel back to the base, but Pitch 1's protection is sparse (5.9+ R) for roughly its first 20 feet, so a forced retreat or fall high on P1 is a serious hazard. Above the technical pitches, the connecting ridge can generally be downclimbed toward the base in most sections if weather turns.

pitch_detail.notes: Face climbs a crisp dihedral just left of the pinnacle's granite shield, then traverses right ~40 ft across parallel dikes toward the face's edge; effectively unprotected for roughly the first 20 ft, ending in an insecure high-step/mantle crux below a small roof.
Corner/crack climbing up the lower face to a ledge system.
Ledge traverse through a short rock gully to gain the ridge crest.
Roughly 800 ft of ridge-crest climbing, typically simul-climbed or short-pitched, leading toward Mount Challenger's connecting ridge and true summit.

backups.itinerary: Day 1: Drive to the Hannegan Pass Trailhead and hike roughly 16 mi via Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack River ford, Easy Ridge, and the Imperfect Impasse to camp at Perfect Pass (a full day; ~7,000 ft of gain). Day 2: Rope up and cross the Challenger Glacier to the base of Poltergeist Pinnacle (roughly 3 hours from camp per the first-ascent account), climb the East Face route (3 technical pitches plus ~800 ft of simul-climbed ridge), traverse to Mount Challenger's summit, and descend the Challenger Glacier back to Perfect Pass camp. Day 3: Hike out to the trailhead.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge, Perfect Pass and the Challenger Glacier
approach_variants.notes: A multi-day expedition into one of the range's most remote corners with essentially no bail options once committed. From the trailhead at the end of the forest road, the trail climbs steadily through forest to Hannegan Pass, where the maintained tread ends. Drop east into the Chilliwack River valley — the last reliable water for a while — then regain height onto Easy Ridge, a long, partly brushy climbers' route past blueberry meadows and the remains of an old lookout on the ridge high point. From Easy Ridge, contour toward the east flank of the neighbouring peak to the notorious moat-and-cliff notch that cuts the ridge; it often still holds snow well into summer and typically needs a short stretch of low fifth-class downclimbing, or a scramble around or under a snow tunnel, to cross. Beyond it, climb snowfields to Perfect Pass, the standard base camp; whiteout here is a genuine hazard, and parties have set off toward the wrong wall. From Perfect Pass, rope up and traverse east around the Challenger Arm and cross several miles of upper glacier toward the cirque below the south side of the subsidiary summits. In lower-snow years a broken icefall blocks the direct line and most parties detour high above the first crevasse band, or drop back toward the arm for a lower line.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through early September, once the glacier has consolidated enough to cross and before autumn storms return. The first week of August is statistically the driest stretch here. Early-season attempts find more snow on the glacier and on the connecting ridge.
hazards: a severely runout crux pitch with roughly forty feet of essentially unprotectable climbing and groundfall potential
crevassed glacier travel for several miles each way, worse late season and in low-snow years
loose rock and exposed downclimbing at the moat-and-cliff notch on Easy Ridge
icefall hazard near the Challenger Arm and the cirque below
extreme remoteness, with no realistic prospect of quick outside help
approach_variants.baseFinding: A huge shield streaked with dikes like bolts of lightning is the proof, and you can see it from out on the glacier. This is the southernmost of the prominent subsummits on the ridge between Mount Challenger and Crooked Thumb, and it is identified by one feature rather than by its shape: the base of the tower carries an enormous shield of dark granite crisscrossed by hundreds of pale dikes running across it like bolts of lightning. That streaking is unmistakable and visible from well out on the glacier, so pick the tower off before you commit to a line across the ice. The climbing starts in a clean dihedral just left of the dike-streaked shield, roughly twenty feet above the snow, and the bergschrund or moat at the foot of it is the first thing to assess, because it decides whether that start is reachable at all on the day. If the wall in front of you is uniform dark granite with no lightning-streak dikes, you are beneath the wrong subsummit and should continue south along the base. Once on it, the first pitch tiptoes rightward across parallel dikes for about forty feet to the very edge of the face; that stretch takes essentially no protection and a fall on it is long, with cracks only appearing higher up.

bivy.name: Challenger Arm camp
bivy.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.
bivy.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
bivy.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
bivy.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. Walk-up only and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. Closed under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

bivy.name: Beaver Pass Camp
bivy.notes: A broad forested saddle about thirteen miles up from Ross Lake, and the jumping-off point for Wiley Ridge, which is the walking line onto the Challenger Glacier from the east. It is the largest camp on this side, with group and stock capacity, so it absorbs parties too big for the four-person camps below. A 1938 log shelter listed on the National Register stands at the pass; treat it as a historic structure rather than as shelter you can rely on. Because the camp sits on a divide rather than in a creek bottom, tank up lower down if the season has been dry.
bivy.water: Seasonal source near the saddle; the least dependable water on the Big Beaver trail and it can run thin in a dry late summer
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
bivy.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites

bivy.name: Eiley Lake benches, lower Wiley Ridge
bivy.notes: The first real camp on the eastern walking approach to Mount Challenger, roughly six hours along the ridge from Beaver Pass. Parties climbing Challenger from this side commonly use it for two nights, going to the summit and back on the middle day rather than moving camp, because the ridge is slow going in both directions. The terrain opens out of the timber into heather at about 5,200 ft and the walking improves from there. Below treeline expect insects and plan on a tent or a properly sealed bivy bag rather than sleeping out. Important: the whole Big Beaver approach that feeds this ridge sits inside the 2026 fire closure, so confirm the trail and Beaver Pass are open before planning around it.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and snowmelt in the hollows around it. This is the last dependable water for a long stretch of ridge, so tank up here rather than counting on anything higher.
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required, and this is cross-country ground rather than a designated camp — ask at the counter which zone the night is being written into, because the ridge straddles more than one. Walk-up only. No fires. Bury waste in a cathole below the snowline and carry it out above.
bivy.capacity: Two or three small parties spread along the benches; party limit 6

bivy.name: East Wiley Basin and the Wiley Lake benches, upper Wiley Ridge
bivy.notes: The upper half of Wiley Ridge, on the south-facing side, and the last bivouac ground before the glacier. A party that gets this far on the second day has a genuinely short summit day left: the ridge rolls over a gentle knoll near 7,100 ft past Wiley Lake and then reaches Challenger Gap at the edge of the Challenger Glacier. Camping here rather than at Eiley Lake is the difference between a long summit day and a reasonable one, and it is the sensible base for Poltergeist Pinnacle, which needs the early start that a technical face demands. The ridge is deceptively slow — five miles as the crow flies feels like double that with the constant rise and fall — so parties routinely need a night lower down as well as this one.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns. Wiley Lake is rimmed by ice and holds water well into the season, but the basin's tarns are seasonal and a late-summer party should expect to hunt or melt.
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the appropriate cross-country zone, walk-up only. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and stay out of the heather meadows — this is the surface rule the park actually enforces up here. Fires prohibited, waste out in a blue bag once on snow.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on gravel and heather benches; party limit 6
